A tool called `effigy` takes a source file from some **original problem domain** and rewrites or obscures it so the file can be sent to a third-party model for architectural review without revealing what the original code was about. You are that third party, and you are hostile. You have **complete knowledge of the tool**. It is a public research repository: its algorithms, its configuration, and its prompts are all published. Assume nothing is secret except the original source itself. Specifically: Solution `llm-translation` — whole-file rewrite into a different problem domain by a language model. A local or hosted model is given the file and instructed to rewrite it into a target domain. The system prompt is published; its instructions are, in summary: rename every module, package, class, function, method, variable, parameter, field and constant; rewrite every string literal, comment and docstring into the target domain; replace every acronym, data literal, proper noun, URL, file path, table and column name; but **preserve the architecture exactly** — same control flow, same function count and arity, same class hierarchy, same coupling, same dead code, same god-objects, same dependency cycles, same comment positions and speech acts, same naming morphology, same length. It is explicitly told not to fix bugs, remove duplication, or improve the code, because the defects are the object of study. The only names it is told to leave alone are those the language owns: keywords, builtins, standard-library symbols, and public third-party package APIs.
